entries.e3e70bd66a76fcf44efaca7740f44e36ae1b345b: <div sID="gen9344" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="6" osisID="Job.6" sID="Job.6"/> <div eID="gen9344" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9345" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen9346" type="x-p"/> Eliphaz concluded his discourse with an air of assurance; very confident he was that what he had said was so plain and so pertinent that nothing could be objected in answer to it. But, though he that is first in his own cause seems just, yet his neighbour comes and searches him. Job is not convinced by all he had said, but still justifies himself in his complaints and condemns him for the weakness of his arguing. I. He shows that he had just cause to complain as he did of his troubles, and so it would appear to any impartial judge, <reference osisRef="Job.6.2-Job.6.7">ver. 2-7</reference>. II. He continues his passionate wish that he might speedily be cut off by the stroke of death, and so be eased of all his miseries, <reference osisRef="Job.6.8-Job.6.13">ver. 8-13</reference>. III. He reproves his friends for their uncharitable censures of him and their unkind treatment, <reference osisRef="Job.6.14-Job.6.30">ver. 14-30</reference>. It must be owned that Job, in all this, spoke much that was reasonable, but with a mixture of passion and human infirmity. And in this contest, as indeed in most contests, there was fault on both sides.
entries.639a8f25b3614bc45dda013416075bbf4eeb839b: <div eID="gen9346" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen9345" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Job's Reply to Eliphaz. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1520.)</title> <div sID="gen9347" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> But Job answered and said, <hi type="super">2</hi> Oh that my grief were thoroughly weighed, and my calamity laid in the balances together! <hi type="super">3</hi> For now it would be heavier than the sand of the sea: therefore my words are swallowed up. <hi type="super">4</hi> For the arrows of the Almighty <hi type="italic">are</hi> within me, the poison whereof drinketh up my spirit: the terrors of God do set themselves in array against me. <hi type="super">5</hi> Doth the wild ass bray when he hath grass? or loweth the ox over his fodder? <hi type="super">6</hi> Can that which is unsavoury be eaten without salt? or is there <hi type="italic">any</hi> taste in the white of an egg? <hi type="super">7</hi> The things <hi type="italic">that</hi> my soul refused to touch <hi type="italic">are</hi> as my sorrowful meat. <div eID="gen9347" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9348" type="x-p"/> Eliphaz, in the beginning of his discourse, had been very sharp upon Job, and yet it does not appear that Job gave him any interruption, but heard him patiently till he had said all he had to say. Those that would make an impartial judgment of a discourse must hear it out, and take it entire. But, when he had concluded, he makes his reply, in which he speaks very feelingly. <div eID="gen9348" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9349" type="x-p"/> I. He represents his calamity, in general, as much heavier than either he had expressed it or they had apprehended it, <reference osisRef="Job.6.2-Job.6.3">v. 2, 3</reference>. He could not fully describe it; they would not fully apprehend it, or at least would not own that they did; and therefore he would gladly appeal to a third person, who had just weights and just balances with which to weigh his grief and calamity, and would do it with an impartial hand. He wished that they would set his grief and all the expressions of it in one scale, his calamity and all the particulars of it in the other, and (though he would not altogether justify himself in his grief) they would find (as he says, <reference osisRef="Job.23.2">ch. xxiii. 2</reference>) that <hi type="italic">his stroke was heavier than his groaning;</hi> for, whatever his grief was, his calamity was <hi type="italic">heavier than the sand of the sea:</hi> it was complicated, it was aggravated, every grievance weighty, and all together numerous as the sand. "Therefore (says he) <hi type="italic">my words are swallowed up;</hi>" that is, "Therefore you must excuse both the brokenness and the bitterness of my expressions. Do not think it strange if my speech be not so fine and polite as that of an eloquent orator, or so grave and regular as that of a morose philosopher: no, in these circumstances I can pretend neither to the one nor to the other; my words are, as I am, quite swallowed up." Now, 1. He hereby complains of it as his unhappiness that his friends undertook to administer spiritual physic to him before they thoroughly understood his case and knew the worst of it. It is seldom that those who are at ease themselves rightly weigh the afflictions of the afflicted. Every one feels most from his own burden; few feel from other people's. 2. He excuses the passionate expressions he had used when he cursed his day. Though he could not himself justify all he had said, yet he thought his friends should not thus violently condemn it, for really the case was extraordinary, and that might be connived at in such a man of sorrows as he now was which in any common grief would by no means be allowed. 3. He bespeaks the charitable and compassionate sympathy of his friends with him, and hopes, by representing the greatness of his calamity, to bring them to a better temper towards him. To those that are pained it is some ease to be pitied. <div eID="gen9349" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9350" type="x-p"/> II. He complains of the trouble and terror of mind he was in as the sorest part of his calamity, <reference osisRef="Job.6.4">v. 4</reference>. Herein he was a type of Christ, who, in his sufferings, complained most of the sufferings of his soul. <hi type="italic">Now is my soul troubled,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.12.27">John xii. 27</reference>. <hi type="italic">My soul is exceedingly sorrowful,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.26.38">Matt. xxvi. 38</reference>. <hi type="italic">My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.27.46">Matt. xxvii. 46</reference>. Poor Job sadly complains here, 1. Of what he felt <hi type="italic">The arrows of the Almighty are within me.</hi> It was not so much the troubles themselves he was under that put him into this confusion, his poverty, disgrace, and bodily pain; but that which cut him to the heart and put him into this agitation, was to think that the God he loved and served had brought all this upon him and laid him under these marks of his displeasure. Note, Trouble of mind is the sorest trouble. <hi type="italic">A wounded spirit who can bear!</hi> Whatever burden of affliction, in body or estate, God is pleased to lay upon us, we may well afford to submit to it as long as he continues to the use of our reason and the peace of our consciences; but, if in either of these we be disturbed, our case is sad indeed and very pitiable. The way to prevent God's fiery darts of trouble is with the shield of faith to quench Satan's fiery darts of temptation. Observe, He calls them the <hi type="italic">arrows of the Almighty;</hi> for it is an instance of the power of God above that of any man that he can with his arrows reach the soul. He that made the soul can make his sword to approach to it. The poison or heat of these arrows is said to drink up his spirit, because it disturbed his reason, shook his resolution, exhausted his vigour, and threatened his life; and therefore his passionate expressions, though they could not be justified, might be excused. 2. Of what he feared. He saw himself charged by <hi type="italic">the terrors of God,</hi> as by an army set in battle-array, and surrounded by them. God, by his terrors, fought against him. As he had no comfort when he retired inward into his own bosom, so he had none when he looked upward towards Heaven. He that used to be encouraged with the consolations of God not only wanted those, but was amazed with the terrors of God. <div eID="gen9350" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9351" type="x-p"/> III. He reflects upon his friends for their severe censures of his complaints and their unskilful management of his case. 1. Their reproofs were causeless. He complained, it is true, now that he was in this affliction, but he never used to complain, as those do who are of a fretful unquiet spirit, when he was in prosperity: he did not <hi type="italic">bray when he had grass,</hi> nor <hi type="italic">low over his fodder,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.6.5">v. 5</reference>. But, now that he was utterly deprived of all his comforts, he must be a stock or a stone, and not have the sense of an ox or a wild ass, if he did not give some vent to his grief. He was forced to eat unsavoury meats, and was so poor that he had not a grain of salt wherewith to season them, nor to give a little taste to the white of an egg, which was now the choicest dish he had at his table, <reference osisRef="Job.6.6">v. 6</reference>. Even that food which once he would have scorned to touch he was now glad of, and it was his <hi type="italic">sorrowful meat,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.6.7">v. 7</reference>. Note, It is wisdom not to use ourselves or our children to be nice and dainty about meat and drink, because we know not how we or they may be reduced, nor how that which we now disdain may be made acceptable by necessity. 2. Their comforts were sapless and insipid; so some understand <reference osisRef="Job.6.6-Job.6.7">v. 6, 7</reference>. He complains he had nothing now offered to him for his relief that was proper for him, no cordial, nothing to revive and cheer his spirits; what they had afforded was in itself as tasteless as the white of an egg, and, when applied to him, as loathsome and burdensome as the most sorrowful meat. I am sorry he should say thus of what Eliphaz had excellently well said, <reference osisRef="Job.5.8-Job.5.13">ch. v. 8</reference>, &c. But peevish spirits are too apt thus to abuse their comforters.
entries.aaffc756bb0bd325254746aa48ac3bf3f770b081: <div eID="gen9351" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9352" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">8</hi> Oh that I might have my request; and that God would grant <hi type="italic">me</hi> the thing that I long for! <hi type="super">9</hi> Even that it would please God to destroy me; that he would let loose his hand, and cut me off! <hi type="super">10</hi> Then should I yet have comfort; yea, I would harden myself in sorrow: let him not spare; for I have not concealed the words of the Holy One. <hi type="super">11</hi> What <hi type="italic">is</hi> my strength, that I should hope? and what <hi type="italic">is</hi> mine end, that I should prolong my life? <hi type="super">12</hi> <hi type="italic">Is</hi> my strength the strength of stones? or <hi type="italic">is</hi> my flesh of brass? 13 <hi type="italic">Is</hi> not my help in me? and is wisdom driven quite from me? <div eID="gen9352" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9353" type="x-p"/> Ungoverned passion often grows more violent when it meets with some rebuke and check. The troubled sea rages most when it dashes against a rock. Job had been courting death, as that which would be the happy period of his miseries, <reference osisRef="Job.3.1-Job.3.26">ch. iii</reference>. For this Eliphaz had gravely reproved him, but he, instead of unsaying what he had said, says it here again with more vehemence than before; and it is as ill said as almost any thing we meet with in all his discourses, and is recorded for our admonition, not our imitation. <div eID="gen9353" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9354" type="x-p"/> I. He is still most passionately desirous to die, as if it were not possible that he should ever see good days again in this world, or that, by the exercise of grace and devotion, he might make even these days of affliction good days. He could see no end of his trouble but death, and had not patience to wait the time appointed for that. He has a request to make; there is a thing he longs for (<reference osisRef="Job.6.8">v. 8</reference>); and what is that? One would think it should be, "That it would please God to deliver me, and restore me to my prosperity again;" no, <hi type="italic">That it would please God to destroy me,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.6.9">v. 9</reference>. "As once he let loose his hand to make me poor, and then to make me sick, let him loose it once more to put an end to my life. Let him give the fatal stroke; it shall be to me the <hi type="italic">coup de grace—the stroke of favour,</hi>" as, in France, they call the last blow which dispatches those that are broken on the wheel. There was a time when <hi type="italic">destruction from the Almighty was a terror</hi> to Job (<reference osisRef="Job.31.23">ch. xxxi. 23</reference>), yet now he courts the destruction of the flesh, but in hopes that the spirit should be saved in the day of the Lord Jesus. Observe, Though Job was extremely desirous of death, and very angry at its delays, yet he did not offer to destroy himself, nor to take away his own life, only he begged <hi type="italic">that it would please God to destroy him.</hi> Seneca's morals, which recommend self-murder as the lawful redress of insupportable grievances, were not then known, nor will ever be entertained by any that have the least regard to the law of God and nature. How uneasy soever the soul's confinement in the body may be, it must by no means break prison, but wait for a fair discharge. <div eID="gen9354" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9355" type="x-p"/> II. He puts this desire into a prayer, that God would grant him this request, that it would please God to do this for him. It was his sin so passionately to desire the hastening of his own death, and offering up that desire to God made it no better; nay, what looked ill in his wish looked worse in his prayer, for we ought not to ask any thing of God but what we can ask in faith, and we cannot ask any thing in faith but what is agreeable to the will of God. Passionate prayers are the worst of passionate expressions, for we should <hi type="italic">lift up pure hands without wrath.</hi> <div eID="gen9355" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9356" type="x-p"/> III. He promises himself effectual relief, and the redress of all his grievances, by the stroke of death (<reference osisRef="Job.6.10">v. 10</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Then should I yet have comfort,</hi> which now I have not, nor ever expect till then." See, 1. The vanity of human life; so uncertain a good is it that it often proves men's greatest burden and nothing is so desirable as to get clear of it. Let grace make us willing to part with it whenever God calls; for it may so happen that even sense may make us desirous to part with it before he calls. 2. The hope which the righteous have in their death. If Job had not had a good conscience, he could not have spoken with this assurance of comfort on the other side death, which turns the tables between the rich man and Lazarus. <hi type="italic">Now he is comforted, and thou art tormented.</hi> <div eID="gen9356" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9357" type="x-p"/> IV. He challenges death to do its worst. If he could not die without the dreadful prefaces of bitter pains and agonies, and strong convulsions, if he must be racked before he be executed, yet, in prospect of dying at last, he would make nothing of dying pangs: "<hi type="italic">I would harden myself in sorrow,</hi> would open my breast to receive death's darts, and not shrink from them. <hi type="italic">Let him not spare;</hi> I desire no mitigation of that pain which will put a happy period to all my pains. Rather than not die, let me die so as to feel myself die." These are passionate words, which might better have been spared. We should soften ourselves in sorrow, that we may receive the good impressions of it, and by the sadness of the countenance our hearts, being made tender, may be made better; but, if we harden ourselves, we provoke God to proceed in his controversy; <hi type="italic">for when he judgeth he will overcome.</hi> It is great presumption to dare the Almighty, and to say, <hi type="italic">Let him not spare;</hi> for <hi type="italic">are we stronger than he?</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.10.22">1 Cor. x. 22</reference>. We are much indebted to sparing mercy; it is bad indeed with us when we are weary of that. Let us rather say with David, <hi type="italic">O spare me a little.</hi> <div eID="gen9357" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9358" type="x-p"/> V. He grounds his comfort upon the testimony of his conscience for him that he had been faithful and firm to his profession of religion, and in some degree useful and serviceable to the glory of God in his generation: <hi type="italic">I have not concealed the words of the Holy One.</hi> Observe, 1. Job had the words of the Holy One committed to him. The people of God were at that time blessed with divine revelation. 2. It was his comfort that he had not concealed them, had not received the grace of God therein in vain. (1.) He had not kept them from himself, but had given them full scope to operate upon him, and in every thing to guide and govern him. He had not stifled his convictions, <hi type="italic">imprisoned the truth in unrighteousness,</hi> nor done any thing to hinder the digestion of this spiritual food and the operation of this spiritual physic. Let us never conceal God's word from ourselves, but always receive it in the light of it. (2.) He had not kept them to himself, but had been ready, on all occasions, to communicate his knowledge for the good of others, was never ashamed nor afraid to own the word of God to be his rule, nor remiss in his endeavours to bring others into an acquaintance with it. Note Those, and those only, may promise themselves comfort in death who are good, and do good, while they live. <div eID="gen9358" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9359" type="x-p"/> VI. He justifies himself, in this extreme desire of death, from the deplorable condition he was now in, <reference osisRef="Job.6.11-Job.6.12">v. 11, 12</reference>. Eliphaz, in the close of his discourse, had put him in hopes that he should yet see a good issue of his troubles; but poor Job puts these cordials away from him, refuses to be comforted, abandons himself to despair, and very ingeniously, yet perversely, argues against the encouragements that were given him. Disconsolate spirits will reason strangely against themselves. In answer to the pleasing prospects Eliphaz had flattered him with, he here intimates, 1. That he had no reason to expect any such thing: "<hi type="italic">What is my strength, that I should hope?</hi> You see how I am weakened and brought low, how unable I am to grapple with my distempers, and therefore what reason have I to hope that I should out-live them, and see better days? <hi type="italic">Is my strength the strength of stones?</hi> Are my muscles brass and my sinews steel? No, they are not, and therefore I cannot hold out always in this pain and misery, but must needs sink under the load. Had I strength to grapple with my distemper, I might hope to look through it; but, alas! I have not. The <hi type="italic">weakening of my strength in the way</hi> will certainly be the <hi type="italic">shortening of my days,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Ps.102.23">Ps. cii. 23</reference>. Note, All things considered, we have no reason to reckon upon the long continuance of life in this world. <hi type="italic">What is our strength?</hi> It is depending strength. We have no more strength than God gives us; for in him we live and move. It is decaying strength; we are daily spending the stock, and by degrees it will be exhausted. It is disproportionable to the encounters we may meet with; what is our strength to be depended upon, when two or three days' sickness will make us weak as water? Instead of expecting a long life, we have reason to wonder that we have lived hitherto and to feel that we are hastening off apace. 2. That he had no reason to desire any such thing: "<hi type="italic">What is my end, that I should desire to prolong my life?</hi> What comfort can I promise myself in life, comparable to the comfort I promise myself in death?" Note, Those who, through grace, are ready for another world, cannot see much to invite their stay in this world, or to make them fond of it. That, if it be God's will, we may do him more service and may get to be fitter and riper for heaven, is an end for which we may wish the prolonging of life, in subservience to our chief end; but, otherwise, what can we propose to ourselves in desiring to tarry here? The longer life is the more grievous will its burdens be (<reference osisRef="Eccl.12.1">Eccl. xii. 1</reference>), and the longer life is the less pleasant will be its delights, <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.34-2Sam.19.35">2 Sam. xix. 34, 35</reference>. We have already seen the best of this world, but we are not sure that we have seen the worst of it. <div eID="gen9359" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9360" type="x-p"/> VII. He obviates the suspicion of his being delirious (<reference osisRef="Job.6.13">v. 13</reference>): <hi type="italic">Is not my help in me?</hi> that is, "Have I not the use of my reason, with which, I thank God, I can help myself, though you do not help me? Do you think wisdom is driven quite from me, and that I am gone distracted? No, I am not mad, most noble Eliphaz, but <hi type="italic">speak the words of truth and soberness.</hi>" Note, Those who have grace in them, who have the evidence of it and have it in exercise, have wisdom in them, which will be their help in the worst of times. <hi type="italic">Sat lucis intus—They have light within.</hi>
entries.9df18a0e43b60da0869861317e5f8936dfdf6b14: <div eID="gen9360" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9361" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">14</hi> To him that is afflicted pity <hi type="italic">should be showed</hi> from his friend; but he forsaketh the fear of the Almighty. <hi type="super">15</hi> My brethren have dealt deceitfully as a brook, <hi type="italic">and</hi> as the stream of brooks they pass away; <hi type="super">16</hi> Which are blackish by reason of the ice, <hi type="italic">and</hi> wherein the snow is hid: <hi type="super">17</hi> What time they wax warm, they vanish: when it is hot, they are consumed out of their place. <hi type="super">18</hi> The paths of their way are turned aside; they go to nothing, and perish. <hi type="super">19</hi> The troops of Tema looked, the companies of Sheba waited for them. <hi type="super">20</hi> They were confounded because they had hoped; they came thither, and were ashamed. <hi type="super">21</hi> For now ye are nothing; ye see <hi type="italic">my</hi> casting down, and are afraid. <div eID="gen9361" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9362" type="x-p"/> Eliphaz had been very severe in his censures of Job; and his companions, though as yet they had said little, yet had intimated their concurrence with him. Their unkindness therein poor Job here complains of, as an aggravation of his calamity and a further excuse of his desire to die; for what satisfaction could he ever expect in this world when those that should have been his comforters thus proved his tormentors? <div eID="gen9362" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9363" type="x-p"/> I. He shows what reason he had to expect kindness from them. His expectation was grounded upon the common principles of humanity (<reference osisRef="Job.6.14">v. 14</reference>): "<hi type="italic">To him that is afflicted,</hi> and that is wasting and melting under his affliction, <hi type="italic">pity should be shown from his friend;</hi> and he that does not show that pity <hi type="italic">forsakes the fear of the Almighty.</hi>" Note, 1. Compassion is a debt owing to those that are in affliction. The least which those that are at ease can do for those that are pained and in anguish is to pity them,—to manifest the sincerity of a tender concern for them, and to sympathize with them,—to take cognizance of their case, enquire into their grievances, hear their complaints, and mingle their tears with theirs,—to comfort them, and to do all they can to help and relieve them: this well becomes the members of the same body, who should feel for the grievances of their fellow-members, not knowing how soon the same may be their own. 2. Inhumanity is impiety and irreligion. <hi type="italic">He that withholds compassion from his friend forsakes the fear of the Almighty.</hi> So the Chaldee. <hi type="italic">How dwells the love of God in that man?</hi> <reference osisRef="1John.3.17">1 John iii. 17</reference>. Surely those have no fear of the rod of God upon themselves who have no compassion for those that feel the smart of it. See <reference osisRef="Jas.1.27">Jam. i. 27</reference>. 3. Troubles are the trials of friendship. When a man is afflicted he will see who are his friends indeed and who are but pretenders; for <hi type="italic">a brother is born for adversity,</hi> <reference osisRef="Pr.17.17">Prov. xvii. 17</reference>; <reference osisRef="18.24">xviii. 24</reference>. <div eID="gen9363" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9364" type="x-p"/> II. He shows how wretchedly he was disappointed in his expectations from them (<reference osisRef="Job.6.15">v. 15</reference>): "<hi type="italic">My brethren,</hi> who should have helped me, <hi type="italic">have dealt deceitfully as a brook.</hi>" They came by appointment, with a great deal of ceremony, to mourn with him and to comfort him (<reference osisRef="Job.2.11">ch. ii. 11</reference>); and some extraordinary things were expected from such wise, learned, knowing men, and Job's particular friends. None questioned but that the drift of their discourses would be to comfort Job with the remembrance of his former piety, the assurance of God's favour to him, and the prospect of a glorious issue; but, instead of this, they most barbarously fall upon him with their reproaches and censures, condemn him as a hypocrite, insult over his calamities, and pour vinegar, instead of oil, into his wounds, and thus they deal deceitfully with him. Note, It is fraud and deceit not only to violate our engagements to our friends, but to frustrate their just expectations from us, especially the expectations we have raised. Note, further, It is our wisdom to cease from man. We cannot expect too little from the creature nor too much from the Creator. It is no new thing even for brethren to <hi type="italic">deal deceitfully</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.9.4-Jer.9.5">Jer. ix. 4, 5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.7.5">Mic. vii. 5</reference>); let us therefore put our confidence in the rock of ages, not in broken reeds-in the fountain of life, not in broken cisterns. God will out-do our hopes as much as men come short of them. This disappointment which Job met with he here illustrates by the failing of brooks in summer. <div eID="gen9364" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9365" type="x-p"/> 1. The similitude is very elegant, <reference osisRef="Job.6.15-Job.6.20">v. 15-20</reference>. (1.) Their pretensions are fitly compared to the great show which the brooks make when they are swollen with the waters of a land flood, by the melting of the ice and snow, which make them blackish or muddy, <reference osisRef="Job.6.16">v. 16</reference>. (2.) His expectations from them, which their coming so solemnly to comfort him had raised, he compares to the expectation which the weary thirsty travellers have of finding water in the summer where they have often seen it in great abundance in the winter, <reference osisRef="Job.6.19">v. 19</reference>. <hi type="italic">The troops of Tema and Sheba,</hi> the caravans of the merchants of those countries, whose road lay through the deserts of Arabia, looked and waited for supply of water from those brooks. "Hard by here," says one, "A little further," says another, "when I last travelled this way, there was water enough; we shall have that to refresh us." Where we have met with relief or comfort we are apt to expect it again; and yet it does not follow; for, (3.) The disappointment of his expectation is here compared to the confusion which seizes the poor travellers when they find heaps of sand where they expected floods of water. In the winter, when they were not thirsty, there was water enough. Every one will applaud and admire those that are full and in prosperity. But in the heat of summer, when they needed water, then it failed them; it was consumed (<reference osisRef="Job.6.17">v. 17</reference>); it was turned aside, <reference osisRef="Job.6.18">v. 18</reference>. When those who are rich and high are sunk and impoverished, and stand in need of comfort, then those who before gathered about them stand aloof from them, those who before commended them are forward to run them down. Thus those who raise their expectations high from the creature will find it fail them when it should help them; whereas those who make God their confidence have help <hi type="italic">in the time of need,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.4.16">Heb. iv. 16</reference>. Those who make gold their hope will sooner or later be ashamed of it, and of their confidence in it (<reference osisRef="Ezek.7.19">Ezek. vii. 19</reference>); and the greater their confidence was the greater their shame will be: <hi type="italic">They were confounded because they had hoped,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.6.20">v. 20</reference>. We prepare confusion for ourselves by our vain hopes: the reeds break under us because we lean upon them. If we build a house upon the sand, we shall certainly be confounded, for it will fall in the storm, and we must thank ourselves for being such fools as to expect it would stand. We are not deceived unless we deceive ourselves. <div eID="gen9365" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9366" type="x-p"/> 2. The application is very close (<reference osisRef="Job.6.21">v. 21</reference>): <hi type="italic">For now you are nothing.</hi> They seemed to be somewhat, but in conference they added nothing to him. Allude to <reference osisRef="Gal.2.6">Gal. ii. 6</reference>. He was never the wiser, never the better, for the visit they made him. Note, Whatever complacency we may take, or whatever confidence we may put, in creatures, how great soever they may seem and how dear soever they may be to us, one time or other we shall say of them, <hi type="italic">Now you are nothing.</hi> When Job was in prosperity his friends were something to him, he took complacency in them and their society; but "<hi type="italic">Now you are nothing,</hi> now I can find no comfort but in God." It were well for us if we had always such convictions of the vanity of the creature, and its insufficiency to make us happy, as we have sometimes had, or shall have on a sick-bed, a death-bed, or in trouble of conscience: "<hi type="italic">Now you are nothing.</hi> You are not what you have been, what you should be, what you pretend to be, what I thought you would have been; <hi type="italic">for you see my casting down and are afraid.</hi> When you saw me in my elevation you caressed me; but now that you see me in my dejection you are shy of me, are afraid of showing yourselves kind, lest I should thereby be emboldened to beg something of you, or to borrow" (compare <reference osisRef="Job.6.22">v. 22</reference>); "you are afraid lest, if you own me, you should be obliged to keep me." Perhaps they were afraid of catching his distemper or of coming within smell of the noisomeness of it. It is not good, either out of pride or niceness, for love of our purses or of our bodies, to be shy of those who are in distress and afraid of coming near them. Their case may soon be our own.
entries.e13643c65c71fcb42625e450ea913816412737b8: <div eID="gen9366" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9367" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">22</hi> Did I say, Bring unto me? or, Give a reward for me of your substance? <hi type="super">23</hi> Or, Deliver me from the enemy's hand? or, Redeem me from the hand of the mighty? <hi type="super">24</hi> Teach me, and I will hold my tongue: and cause me to understand wherein I have erred. <hi type="super">25</hi> How forcible are right words! but what doth your arguing reprove? <hi type="super">26</hi> Do ye imagine to reprove words, and the speeches of one that is desperate, <hi type="italic">which are</hi> as wind? 27 Yea, ye overwhelm the fatherless, and ye dig <hi type="italic">a pit</hi> for your friend. <hi type="super">28</hi> Now therefore be content, look upon me; for <hi type="italic">it is</hi> evident unto you if I lie. <hi type="super">29</hi> Return, I pray you, let it not be iniquity; yea, return again, my righteousness <hi type="italic">is</hi> in it. <hi type="super">30</hi> Is there iniquity in my tongue? cannot my taste discern perverse things? <div eID="gen9367" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9368" type="x-p"/> Poor Job goes on here to upbraid his friends with their unkindness and the hard usage they gave him. He here appeals to themselves concerning several things which tended both to justify him and to condemn them. If they would but think impartially, and speak as they thought, they could not but own, <div eID="gen9368" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9369" type="x-p"/> I. That, though he was necessitous, yet he was not craving, nor burdensome to his friends. Those that are so, whose troubles serve them to beg by, are commonly less pitied than the silent poor. Job would be glad to see his friends, but he did not say, <hi type="italic">Bring unto me</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.6.22">v. 22</reference>), or, <hi type="italic">Deliver me,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.6.23">v. 23</reference>. He did not desire to put them to any expense, did not urge his friends either, 1. To make a collection for him, to set him up again in the world. Though he could plead that his losses came upon him by the hand of God and not by any fault or folly of his own,—that he was utterly ruined and impoverished,—that he had lived in good condition, and that when he had wherewithal he was charitable and ready to help those that were in distress,—that his friends were rich, and able to help him, yet he did not say, <hi type="italic">Give me of your substance.</hi> Note, A good man, when troubled himself, is afraid of being troublesome to his friends. Or, 2. To raise the country for him, to help him to recover his cattle out of the hands of the Sabeans and Chaldeans, or to make reprisals upon them: "Did I send for you to <hi type="italic">deliver me out of the hand of the mighty?</hi> No, I never expected you should either expose yourselves to any danger or put yourselves to any charge upon my account. I will rather sit down content under my affliction, and make the best of it, than sponge upon my friends." St. Paul worked with his hands, that he might not be burdensome to any. Job's not asking their help did not excuse them from offering it when he needed it and it was in the power of their hands to give it; but it much aggravated their unkindness when he desired no more from them than a good look, and a good word, and yet could not obtain them. It often happens that from man, even when we expect little, we have less, but from God, even when we expect much, we have more, <reference osisRef="Eph.3.20">Eph. iii. 20</reference>. <div eID="gen9369" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9370" type="x-p"/> II. That, though he differed in opinion from them, yet he was not obstinate, but ready to yield to conviction, and to strike sail to truth as soon as ever it was made to appear to him that he was in an error (<reference osisRef="Job.6.24-Job.6.25">v. 24, 25</reference>): "If, instead of invidious reflections and uncharitable insinuations, you will give me plain instructions and solid arguments, which shall carry their own evidence along with them, I am ready to acknowledge my error and own myself in a fault: <hi type="italic">Teach me, and I will hold my tongue;</hi> for I have often found, with pleasure and wonder, <hi type="italic">how forcible right words are.</hi> But the method you take will never make proselytes: <hi type="italic">What doth your arguing reprove?</hi> Your hypothesis is false, your surmises are groundless, your management is weak, and your application peevish and uncharitable." Note, 1. Fair reasoning has a commanding power, and it is a wonder if men are not conquered by it; but railing and foul language are impotent and foolish, and it is no wonder if men are exasperated and hardened by them. 2. It is the undoubted character of every honest man that he is truly desirous to have his mistakes rectified, and to be made to understand wherein he has erred; and he will acknowledge that right words, when they appear to him to be so, though contrary to his former sentiments, are both forcible and acceptable. <div eID="gen9370" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9371" type="x-p"/> III. That, though he had been indeed in a fault, yet they ought not to have given him such hard usage (<reference osisRef="Job.6.26-Job.6.27">v. 26, 27</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Do you imagine,</hi> or contrive with a great deal of art" (for so the word signifies), "<hi type="italic">to reprove words,</hi> some passionate expressions of mine in this desperate condition, as if they were certain indications of reigning impiety and atheism? A little candour and charity would have served to excuse them, and to put a better construction upon them. Shall a man's spiritual state be judged of by some rash and hasty words, which a surprising trouble extorts from him? Is it fair, is it kind, is it just, to criticize in such a case? Would you yourselves be served thus?" Two things aggravated their unkind treatment of him:—1. That they took advantage of his weakness and the helpless condition he was in: <hi type="italic">You overwhelm the fatherless,</hi> a proverbial expression, denoting that which is most barbarous and inhuman. "The fatherless cannot secure themselves from insults, which emboldens men of base and sordid spirits to insult them and trample upon them; and you do so by me." Job, being a childless father, thought himself as much exposed to injury as a fatherless child (<reference osisRef="Ps.127.5">Ps. cxxvii. 5</reference>) and had reason to be offended with those who therefore triumphed over him. Let those who overwhelm and overpower such as upon any account may be looked upon as fatherless know that therein they not only put off the compassions of man, but fight against the compassions of God, who is, and will be, a Father of the fatherless and a helper of the helpless. 2. That they made a pretence of kindness: "<hi type="italic">You dig a pit for your friend;</hi> not only you are unkind to me, who am your friend, but, under colour of friendship, you ensnare me." When they came to see and sit with him he thought he might speak his mind freely to them, and that the more bitter his complaints to them were the more they would endeavour to comfort him. This made him take a greater liberty than otherwise he would have done. David, though he smothered his resentments when the wicked were before him, would probably have given vent to them if none had been by but friends, <reference osisRef="Ps.39.1">Ps. xxxix. 1</reference>. But this freedom of speech, which their professions of concern for him made him use, had exposed him to their censures, and so they might be said to dig a pit for him. Thus, when our hearts are hot within us, what is ill done we are apt to misrepresent as if done designedly. <div eID="gen9371" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9372" type="x-p"/> IV. That, though he had let fall some passionate expressions, yet in the main he was in the right, and that his afflictions, though very extraordinary, did not prove him to be a hypocrite or a wicked man. His righteousness he holds fast, and will not let it go. For the evincing of it he here appeals, 1. To what they saw in him (<reference osisRef="Job.6.28">v. 28</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Be content,</hi> and <hi type="italic">look upon me;</hi> what do you see in me that bespeaks me either a madman or a wicked man? Nay, look in my face, and you may discern there the indications of a patient and submissive spirit, for all this. Let the show of my countenance witness for me that, though I have cursed my day, I do not curse my God." Or rather, "Look upon my ulcers and sore boils, and by them it will be evident to you that I do not lie," that is, "that I do not complain without cause. Let your own eyes convince you that my condition is very sad, and that I do not quarrel with God by making it worse than it is." 2. To what they heard from him, <reference osisRef="Job.6.30">v. 30</reference>. "You hear what I have to say: <hi type="italic">Is there iniquity in my tongue?</hi> that iniquity that you charge me with? Have I blasphemed God or renounced him? Are not my present arguings right? Do not you perceive, by what I say, that I can discern perverse things? I can discover your fallacies and mistakes, and, if I were myself in an error, I could perceive it. Whatever you think of me, I know what I say." 3. To their own second and sober thoughts (<reference osisRef="Job.6.29">v. 29</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Return, I pray you,</hi> consider the thing over again without prejudice and partiality, and let not the result be iniquity, let it not be an unrighteous sentence; and you will find <hi type="italic">my righteousness is in it,</hi>" that is, "I am in the right in this matter; and, though I cannot keep my temper as I should, I keep my integrity, and have not said, nor done, nor suffered, any thing which will prove me other than an honest man." A just cause desires nothing more than a just hearing, and if need be a re-hearing.  <chapter eID="Job.6"/> <div eID="gen9372" type="x-p"/>

entries.39738dccffd6edc3eecaf4a9392687fb0bac50be: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4554"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 6</title> <div sID="gen6592" type="x-p"/> FIRST SERIES CONTINUED.<div eID="gen6592" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Job.6.1-Job.6.30">Job 6:1-30</reference>. Reply of Job to Eliphaz.</title> <div sID="gen6593" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4554"/><hi type="bold">2. throughly weighed--</hi>Oh, that instead of censuring my complaints when thou oughtest rather to have sympathized with me, thou wouldst accurately compare my sorrow, and my misfortunes; these latter "outweigh in the balance" the former. <div eID="gen6593" type="x-p"/>
entries.3a74ce8da82057c4b68715b791ea270e0eb33d61: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4555"/><div sID="gen6594" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4555"/><hi type="bold">3. the sand--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Prov.27.3">Pr 27:3</reference>).<div eID="gen6594" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6595" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">are swallowed up--</hi>See Margin [that is, "I want words to express my grief"]. But Job plainly is apologizing, not for not having had words enough, but for having spoken too much and too boldly; and the Hebrew is, "to speak rashly" [Umbreit, Gesenius, Rosenmuller]. "Therefore were my words so rash." <div eID="gen6595" type="x-p"/>
entries.4e4f09319154a33b226cc79c88a2b4cdabe2e3ec: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4556"/><div sID="gen6596" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4556"/><hi type="bold">4. arrows ... within me--</hi>have pierced me. A poetic image representing the avenging Almighty armed with bow and arrows (<reference osisRef="Ps.38.2">Psa 38:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.38.3">3</reference>). Here the arrows are poisoned. Peculiarly appropriate, in reference to the burning pains which penetrated, like poison, into the inmost parts--("spirit"; as contrasted with mere surface flesh wounds) of Job's body.<div eID="gen6596" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6597" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">set themselves in array--</hi>a military image (<reference osisRef="Judg.20.33">Jud 20:33</reference>). All the terrors which the divine wrath can muster are set in array against me (<reference osisRef="Isa.42.13">Is 42:13</reference>). <div eID="gen6597" type="x-p"/>
entries.73a5ed9f4fdef7dc4ca5a862057e233f65da5a36: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4557"/><div sID="gen6598" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4557"/>5. Neither wild animals, as the wild ass, nor tame, as the ox, are dissatisfied when well-supplied with food. The braying of the one and the lowing of the other prove distress and want of palatable food. So, Job argues, if he complains, it is not without cause; namely, his pains, which are, as it were, disgusting food, which God feeds him with (end of <reference osisRef="Job.6.7">Job 6:7</reference>). But he should have remembered a rational being should evince a better spirit than the brute. <div eID="gen6598" type="x-p"/>
entries.82035321de997b4122e6b5bf96799e71db865f38: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4558"/><div sID="gen6599" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4558"/><hi type="bold">6. unsavoury--</hi>tasteless, insipid. Salt is a chief necessary of life to an Easterner, whose food is mostly vegetable.<div eID="gen6599" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6600" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the white--</hi>literally, "spittle" (<reference osisRef="1Sam.21.13">1Sa 21:13</reference>), which the white of an egg resembles. <div eID="gen6600" type="x-p"/>
entries.c201344269400d2a22a52810d1d52bd3470db84e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4559"/><div sID="gen6601" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4559"/>7. To "touch" is contrasted with "meat." "My taste refused even to touch it, and yet am I fed with such meat of sickness." The second clause literally, is, "Such is like the sickness of my food." The natural taste abhors even to touch insipid food, and such forms my nourishment. For my sickness is like such nauseous food [Umbreit]. (<reference osisRef="Ps.42.3">Psa 42:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.80.5">80:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.102.9">102:9</reference>). No wonder, then, I complain. <div eID="gen6601" type="x-p"/>
entries.4d3a7bddc02bf95687d4df1ebeb14449375e8ac4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4560"/><div sID="gen6602" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4560"/>8. To desire death is no necessary proof of fitness for death. The ungodly sometimes desire it, so as to escape troubles, without thought of the hereafter. The godly desire it, in order to be with the Lord; but they patiently wait God's will. <div eID="gen6602" type="x-p"/>
entries.5bc5ee091dd3b776d113c334a1b080fd4707dcaf: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4561"/><div sID="gen6603" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4561"/><hi type="bold">9. destroy--</hi>literally, "grind" or "crush" (<reference osisRef="Isa.3.15">Is 3:15</reference>).<div eID="gen6603" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6604" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">let loose his hand--</hi>God had put forth His hand only so far as to wound the surface of Job's flesh (<reference osisRef="Job.1.12">Job 1:12</reference>; 2:6); he wishes that hand to be let loose, so as to wound deeply and vitally.<div eID="gen6604" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6605" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cut me off--</hi>metaphor from a weaver cutting off the web, when finished, from the thrum fastening it to the loom (<reference osisRef="Isa.38.12">Is 38:12</reference>). <div eID="gen6605" type="x-p"/>
entries.0575ad199325b444179320b3bd1c4e6e15b773e0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4562"/><div sID="gen6606" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4562"/><hi type="bold">10. I would harden myself in sorrow--</hi>rather, "I would exult in the pain," if I knew that that pain would hasten my death [Gesenius]. Umbreit translates the Hebrew of "Let Him not spare," as "unsparing"; and joins it with "pain."<div eID="gen6606" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6607" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">concealed--</hi>I have not disowned, in word or deed, the commands of the Holy One (<reference osisRef="Ps.119.46">Psa 119:46</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.20.20">Ac 20:20</reference>). He says this in answer to Eliphaz' insinuation that he is a hypocrite. God is here called "the Holy One," to imply man's reciprocal obligation to be holy, as He is holy (<reference osisRef="Lev.19.2">Le 19:2</reference>). <div eID="gen6607" type="x-p"/>
entries.7dfb2f9ca8b5b240f4490cf90a7607bc45608fae: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4563"/><div sID="gen6608" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4563"/>11. What strength have I, so as to warrant the hope of restoration to health? a hope which Eliphaz had suggested. "And what" but a miserable "end" of life is before me, "that I should" desire to "prolong life"? [Umbreit]. Umbreit and Rosenmuller not so well translate the last words "to be patient." <div eID="gen6608" type="x-p"/>
entries.337bb3d72d48f348557f910dd7be97db293300e1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4564"/><div sID="gen6609" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4564"/>12. Disease had so attacked him that his strength would need to be hard as a stone, and his flesh like brass, not to sink under it. But he has only flesh, like other men. It must, therefore, give way; so that the hope of restoration suggested by Eliphaz is vain (see on <reference osisRef="Job.5.11">Job 5:11</reference>). <div eID="gen6609" type="x-p"/>
entries.fa15ff593bb53bd54f051dbc861e3c0f34e4f1c2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4565"/><div sID="gen6610" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4565"/><hi type="bold">13. Is not my help in me?--</hi>The interrogation is better omitted. "There is no help in me!" For "wisdom," "deliverance" is a better rendering. "And deliverance is driven quite from me." <div eID="gen6610" type="x-p"/>
entries.b637aff197d08a2566803d3e2910b380d6a7af6c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4566"/><div sID="gen6611" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4566"/><hi type="bold">14. pity--</hi>a proverb. Charity is the love which judges indulgently of our fellow men: it is put on a par with truth in <reference osisRef="Prov.3.3">Pr 3:3</reference>, for they together form the essence of moral perfection [Umbreit]. It is the spirit of Christianity (<reference osisRef="1Pet.4.8">1Pe 4:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.13.7">1Co 13:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.10.12">Pr 10:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.17.17">17:17</reference>). If it ought to be used towards all men, much more towards friends. But he who does not use it forsaketh (renounceth) the fear of the Almighty (<reference osisRef="Jas.2.13">Jas 2:13</reference>). <div eID="gen6611" type="x-p"/>
entries.cef49da4a715dbdcfa2da71812102becd101693d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4567"/><div sID="gen6612" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4567"/><hi type="bold">15. Those whom I regarded as "my brethren," from whom I looked for faithfulness in my adversity, have disappointed me, as the streams failing from drought--</hi>wadies of Arabia, filled in the winter, but dry in the summer, which disappoint the caravans expecting to find water there. The fulness and noise of these temporary streams answer to the past large and loud professions of my friends; their dryness in summer, to the failure of the friendship when needed. The Arab proverb says of a treacherous friend, "I trust not in thy torrent" (<reference osisRef="Isa.58.11">Is 58:11</reference>, Margin).<div eID="gen6612" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6613" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">stream of brooks--</hi>rather, "the brook in the ravines which passes away." It has no perpetual spring of water to renew it (unlike "the fountain of living waters," <reference osisRef="Jer.2.13">Jr 2:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.33.16">Is 33:16</reference>, at the end); and thus it passes away as rapidly as it arose. <div eID="gen6613" type="x-p"/>
entries.9872fce55c9358aa60c15ff6273c8f612e442ead: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4568"/><div sID="gen6614" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4568"/><hi type="bold">16. blackish--</hi>literally, "Go as a mourner in black clothing" (<reference osisRef="Ps.34.14">Psa 34:14</reference>). A vivid and poetic image to picture the stream turbid and black with melted ice and snow, descending from the mountains into the valley. In the [second] clause, the snow dissolved is, in the poet's view, "hid" in the flood [Umbreit]. <div eID="gen6614" type="x-p"/>
entries.bb9d74d211447d49e6e10415a7ba4472e6dedb77: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4569"/><div sID="gen6615" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4569"/><hi type="bold">17. wax warm--</hi>rather, "At the time when." ("But they soon wax") [Umbreit]. "they become narrower (flow in a narrower bed), they are silent (cease to flow noisily); in the heat (of the sun) they are consumed or vanish out of their place. First the stream flows more narrowly--then it becomes silent and still; at length every trace of water disappears by evaporation under the hot sun" [Umbreit]. <div eID="gen6615" type="x-p"/>
entries.b0b085ba1d39b15f625dc98822f9e04d4bdbf328: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4570"/><div sID="gen6616" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4570"/><hi type="bold">18. turned aside--</hi>rather, "caravans" (Hebrew, "travellers") turn aside from their way, by circuitous routes, to obtain water. They had seen the brook in spring full of water: and now in the summer heat, on their weary journey, they turn off their road by a devious route to reach the living waters, which they remembered with such pleasure. But, when "they go," it is "into a desert" [Noyes and Umbreit]. Not as English Version, "They go to nothing," which would be a tame repetition of the drying up of the waters in <reference osisRef="Job.6.17">Job 6:17</reference>; instead of waters, they find an "empty wilderness"; and, not having strength to regain their road, bitterly disappointed, they "perish." The terse brevity is most expressive. <div eID="gen6616" type="x-p"/>
entries.b5de48abb478b3c23b46216be72f345b15c9fd28: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4571"/><div sID="gen6617" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4571"/><hi type="bold">19. the troops--</hi>that is, "caravans."<div eID="gen6617" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6618" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Tema--</hi>north of Arabia-Deserta, near the Syrian desert; called from Tema son of Ishmael (<reference osisRef="Gen.25.15">Ge 25:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.21.14">Is 21:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.25.23">Jr 25:23</reference>), still so called by the Arabs. <reference osisRef="Job.6.19">Job 6:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.6.20">20</reference> give another picture of the mortification of disappointed hopes, namely, those of the caravans on the direct road, anxiously awaiting the return of their companions from the distant valley. The mention of the locality whence the caravans came gives living reality to the picture.<div eID="gen6618" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6619" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Sheba--</hi>refers here not to the marauders in North Arabia-Deserta (<reference osisRef="Job.1.15">Job 1:15</reference>), but to the merchants (<reference osisRef="Ezek.27.22">Eze 27:22</reference>) in the south, in Arabia-Felix or Yemen, "afar off" (<reference osisRef="Jer.6.20">Jr 6:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.12.42">Mt 12:42</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.10.28">Ge 10:28</reference>). Caravans are first mentioned in <reference osisRef="Gen.37.25">Ge 37:25</reference>; men needed to travel thus in companies across the desert, for defense against the roving robbers and for mutual accommodation.<div eID="gen6619" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6620" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">The companies ... waited for them--</hi>cannot refer to the caravans who had gone in quest of the waters; for <reference osisRef="Job.6.18">Job 6:18</reference> describes their utter destruction. <div eID="gen6620" type="x-p"/>
entries.db61d2feb63f1ab41e756a9e693d601a1308cef6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4572"/><div sID="gen6621" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4572"/>20. literally, "each had hoped"; namely, that their companions would find water. The greater had been their hopes the more bitter now their disappointment;<div eID="gen6621" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6622" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">they came thither--</hi>to the place.<div eID="gen6622" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6623" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and were ashamed--</hi>literally, "their countenances burn," an Oriental phrase for the shame and consternation of deceived expectation; so "ashamed" as to disappointment (<reference osisRef="Rom.5.5">Ro 5:5</reference>). <div eID="gen6623" type="x-p"/>
entries.2eecc4802256e975e6fbdc3d507b3e1eb64bd3ba: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4573"/><div sID="gen6624" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4573"/>21. As the dried-up brook is to the caravan, so are ye to me, namely, a nothing; ye might as well not be in existence [Umbreit]. The Margin "like to them," or "to it" (namely, the waters of the brook), is not so good a reading.<div eID="gen6624" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6625" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ye see, and are afraid--</hi>Ye are struck aghast at the sight of my misery, and ye lose presence of mind. Job puts this mild construction on their failing to relieve him with affectionate consolation. <div eID="gen6625" type="x-p"/>
entries.1deec2b33ed83ed22fc3c5d00fa94741b25c38d5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4574"/><div sID="gen6626" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4574"/>22. And yet I did not ask you to "bring me" a gift; or to "pay for me out of your substance a reward" (to the Judge, to redeem me from my punishment); all I asked from you was affectionate treatment. <div eID="gen6626" type="x-p"/>
entries.bdb37afb11dd935b97f98b85127cd2c2644e1d00: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4575"/><div sID="gen6627" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4575"/><hi type="bold">23. the mighty--</hi>the oppressor, or creditor, in whose power the debtor was [Umbreit]. <div eID="gen6627" type="x-p"/>
entries.e028cc16b22aa1464bdd6c7cfdf60fb34c47ec30: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4576"/><div sID="gen6628" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4576"/>24-25. Irony. If you can "teach me" the right view, I am willing to be set right, and "hold my tongue"; and to be made to see my error. But then if your words be really the right words, how is it that they are so feeble? "Yet how feeble are the words of what you call the right view." So the Hebrew is used (in <reference osisRef="Mic.2.10">Mi 2:10</reference>; 1:9). The English Version, "How powerful," &c., does not agree so well with the last clause of the verse. <div eID="gen6628" type="x-p"/>
entries.59d8b29cbfeb1a51e0aeae10b066f4f8d74c9c4e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4578"/><div sID="gen6630" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4578"/><hi type="bold">26. Do you imagine--</hi>or, "mean."<div eID="gen6630" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6631" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to reprove words and (to reprove) the speeches of one desperate, (which are) as wind?--</hi>mere nothings, not to be so narrowly taken to task? Umbreit not so well takes the Hebrew for "as wind," as "sentiments"; making formal "sentiments" antithetical to mere "speeches," and supplying, not the word "reprove," but "would you regard," from the first clause. <div eID="gen6631" type="x-p"/>
entries.9e069e6f58e20aabb18ffcdc96a8cbffa9ac3bff: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4579"/><div sID="gen6632" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4579"/>27. literally, "ye cause" (supply, "your anger") [Umbreit], a net, namely, of sophistry [Noyes and Schuttens], to fall upon the desolate (one bereft of help, like the fatherless orphan);<div eID="gen6632" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6633" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and ye dig (a pit) for your friend--</hi>that is, try to ensnare him, to catch him in the use of unguarded language [Noyes]. (<reference osisRef="Ps.57.6">Psa 57:6</reference>); metaphor from hunters catching wild beasts in a pit covered with brushwood to conceal it. Umbreit from the Syriac, and answering to his interpretation of the first clause, has, "Would you be indignant against your friend?" The Hebrew in <reference osisRef="Job.41.6">Job 41:6</reference>, means to "feast upon." As the first clause asks, "Would you catch him in a net?" so this follows up the image, "And would you next feast upon him, and his miseries?" So the Septuagint. <div eID="gen6633" type="x-p"/>
entries.ed1b0ad1612bebb6a330f53e7cb3f159d0dfd8b4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4580"/><div sID="gen6634" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4580"/><hi type="bold">28. be content--</hi>rather, "be pleased to"--look. Since you have so falsely judged my words, look upon me, that is, upon my countenance: for (it is evident before your faces) if I lie; my countenance will betray me, if I be the hypocrite that you suppose. <div eID="gen6634" type="x-p"/>
entries.a5c4c7c5d9b87b226f08908fb2749369314c082e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4581"/><div sID="gen6635" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4581"/><hi type="bold">29. Return--</hi>rather, "retract" your charges:<div eID="gen6635" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6636" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">let it not be iniquity--</hi>that is, (retract) that injustice may not be done me. Yea retract, "my righteousness is in it"; that is, my right is involved in this matter. <div eID="gen6636" type="x-p"/>
entries.8f19c1e1b9a6427fbaf2dc4232188323aca1057c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4582"/><div sID="gen6637" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4582"/>30. Will you say that my guilt lies in the organ of speech, and will you call it to account? or, Is it that my taste (palate) or discernment is not capable to form a judgment of perverse things? Is it thus you will explain the fact of my having no consciousness of guilt? [Umbreit]. <chapter eID="Job.6"/>

entries.ba21ba0ebd2193e20ea199bac81dbbb2eb2f1936: <div eID="gen16086" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen16087" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen16088" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen16088" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen16087" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen16089" type="x-p"/> Job answers, and vindicates himself; and shows that the great affliction which he suffered was the cause of his complaining, by which life was rendered burdensome to him, <reference osisRef="Job.6.1-Job.6.13">Job 6:1-13</reference>. He complains that, whereas he expected consolation from his friends, he had received nothing but the bitterest reproaches, on the assumed ground that he must be a wicked man, else God would not so grievously afflict him, <reference osisRef="Job.6.14-Job.6.20">Job 6:14-20</reference>. He shows them that they knew nothing of his case, and that they had no compassion, <reference osisRef="Job.6.21-Job.6.23">Job 6:21-23</reference>. And then entreats them, if they can, to show him in what he has offended, as he is ready to acknowledge and correct every trespass, <reference osisRef="Job.6.24-Job.6.30">Job 6:24-30</reference>.
entries.acd2d74e553183e14c2bc33a17601e7294f54923: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen16089" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16090" type="x-p"/> O that my grief were thoroughly weighed - Job wished to be dealt with according to justice; as he was willing that his sins, if they could be proved, should be weighed against his sufferings; and if this could not be done, he wished that his sufferings and his complainings might be weighed together; and it would then be seen that, bitter as his complaint had been, it was little when compared with the distress which occasioned it.
entries.cb3c64467d6f9dd804525f5191c74d54640825f1: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen16090" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16091" type="x-p"/> Heavier than the sand of the sea - This includes two ideas: their number was too great to be counted; their weight was too great to be estimated.
entries.0f51f3f8ead06b0ceb6dd00d750428dc255b764c: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen16091" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16092" type="x-p"/> The arrows of the Almighty - There is an evident reference here to wounds inflicted by poisoned arrows; and to the burning fever occasioned by such wounds, producing such an intense parching thirst as to dry up all the moisture in the system, stop all the salivary ducts, thicken and inflame the blood, induce putrescency, and terminate in raging mania, producing the most terrifying images, from which the patient is relieved only by death. This is strongly expressed in the fine figure: The Poison Drinketh Up my Spirit; the Terrors of God Set Themselves in Array against me. That calamities are represented among the Eastern writers as the arrows of the Almighty, we have abundant proofs. In reference to this, I shall adduce that fine saying attributed to Aaly, the son-in-law of Mohammed in the Toozuki Teemour; which I have spoken of elsewhere. "It was once demanded of the fourth califf (Aaly), 'If the canopy of heaven were a bow; and if the earth were the cord thereof; and if calamities were the arrows; if mankind were the mark for those arrows; and if Almighty God, the tremendous and glorious, were the unerring Archer; to whom could the sons of Adam flee for protection?' The califf answered, 'The sons of Adam must flee unto the Lord.'" This fine image Job keeps in view in the eighth and ninth verses, wishing that the unerring marksman may let fly these arrows, let loose his hand, to destroy and cut him off.
entries.3a7418a5bf2f8b7888dd74b10cb483fb65e24c4e: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen16092" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16093" type="x-p"/> Doth the wild ass - פרא pere, translated onager, by the Vulgate, from the ονος αγριος of the Septuagint, which we properly enough, translate wild ass. It is the same with the tame ass; only in a wild state it grows to a larger size, is stronger, and more fleet. The meaning of Job appears to be this: You condemn me for complaining; do I complain without a cause? The wild ass will not bray, and the ox will not low, unless in want. If they have plenty of provender, they are silent. Were I at rest, at ease, and happy, I would not complain.
entries.89feb6ae44eedb50a28a5ac84d083069e1314581: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen16093" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16094" type="x-p"/> Can that which is unsavoury - Mr. Good renders this verse as follows: Doth insipid food without a mixture of salt, yea, doth the white of the egg give forth pungency? Which he thus illustrates: "Doth that which hath nothing of seasoning, nothing of a pungent or irritable power within it, produce pungency or irritation? I too should be quiet and complain not, if I had nothing provocative or acrimonious, but, alas! the food I am doomed to partake of is the very calamity which is most acute to my soul - that which I most loathe, and which is most grievous or trying to my palate." Some render the original, Is there any dependence on the drivel of dreams? There have been a great variety of interpretations given of this verse. I could add another; but that of Mr. Good is as likely to be correct as that of any other critic.
entries.ef7d688ecf139370c7237128a5910d06068b8c7f: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen16094" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16095" type="x-p"/> O that I might have - As Job had no hope that he should ever be redeemed from his present helpless state, he earnestly begs God to shorten it by taking away his life.
entries.9e29516058e31d119a28743ff3f6e4059cdb495f: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen16095" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16096" type="x-p"/> Let loose his hand - A metaphor taken from an archer drawing his arrow to the head, and then loosing his hold, that the arrow may fly to the mark. See on <reference osisRef="Job.6.4">Job 6:4</reference> (note).
entries.78cf6a13803fa7cee62dfdefc1ac5e403edd2aa6: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen16096" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16097" type="x-p"/> Then should I yet have comfort - Instead of עוד od, Yet, three of Kennicott's and De Rossi's MSS. have זאת zoth, This. And This should be my comfort. The expectation that he will speedily make an end of me would cause me to rejoice with great joy. This reading is supported by the Vulgate and the Chaldee. <div eID="gen16097" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16098" type="x-p"/> I would harden myself in sorrow - To know that I should shortly have an end put to my miseries would cause me to endure the present with determinate resolution. Let him not spare - let him use whatever means he chooses, for I will not resist his decree; he is holy, and his decrees must be just.
entries.8ecb2bb44e9692375baf58f52d7c52aecb16247e: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen16098" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16099" type="x-p"/> What is my strength - I can never suppose that my strength will be restored; and, were that possible, have I any comfortable prospect of a happy termination of my life? Had I any prospect of future happiness, I might well bear my present ills; but the state of my body and the state of my circumstances preclude all hope.
entries.76ba9df2c2b76c0ff19bd114725e79a7d7416d68: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen16099" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16100" type="x-p"/> Is my strength the strength of stones? - I am neither a rock, nor is my flesh brass, that I can endure all these calamities. This is a proverbial saying, and exists in all countries. Cicero says, Non enim est e saxo sculptus, aut e Robore dolatus Homo; habet corpus, habet animum; movetur mente, movetur sensibus. "For man is not chiselled out of the rock, nor hewn out of the oak; he has a body, and he has a soul; the one is actuated by intellect, the other by the senses." Quaest. Acad. iv. 31. So Homer, where he represents Apollo urging the Trojans to attack the Greeks: - Νεμεσησε δ' Απολλων, Περγαμου εκκατιδων· Τρωεσσι δε κεκλετ' αυσας· Ορνυσθ', ἱπποδαμοι Τρωες, μηδ' εικετε χαρμης Αργειοις· επει ου σφιλιθος χρως, ουδε σιδηρος, Χαλκον ανασχεσθαι ταμεσιχροα βαλλομενοισιν. <div eID="gen16100" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16101" type="x-p"/> Illiad, lib. iv., ver. 507. <div eID="gen16101" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16102" type="x-p"/> But Phoebus now from Ilion's towering height <div eID="gen16102" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16103" type="x-p"/> Shines forth reveal'd, and animates the fight. <div eID="gen16103" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16104" type="x-p"/> Trojans, be bold, and force to force oppose; <div eID="gen16104" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16105" type="x-p"/> Your foaming steeds urge headlong on the foes! <div eID="gen16105" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16106" type="x-p"/> Nor are their bodies rocks, nor ribb'd with steel; <div eID="gen16106" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16107" type="x-p"/> Your weapons enter, and your strokes they feel. <div eID="gen16107" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16108" type="x-p"/> Pope. <div eID="gen16108" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16109" type="x-p"/> These are almost the same expressions as those in Job.
entries.abb75d269920ab0aac4a1734c5e394f81cc251f1: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen16109" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16110" type="x-p"/> Is not my help in me? - My help is all in myself; and, alas! that is perfect weakness: and my subsistence, תושיה tushiyah, all that is real, stable, and permanent, is driven quite from me. My friends have forsaken me, and I am abandoned to myself; my property is all taken away, and I have no resources left. I believe Job neither said, nor intended to say, as some interpreters have it, Reason is utterly driven from me. Surely there is no mark in this chapter of his being deranged, or at all impaired in his intellect.
entries.bd2e0702fdbbe4d0600f04c55443ad5adb2b5776: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen16110" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16111" type="x-p"/> To him that is afflicted pity should be showed from his friend; but he forsaketh the fear of the Almighty - The Vulgate gives a better sense, Qui tollit ab amico suo misericordiam, timorem Domini dereliquit, "He who takes away mercy from his friend, hath cast off the fear of the Lord." The word למס lammas, which we render to him who is Afflicted, from מסה masah, to dissolve, or waste away, is in thirty-two of Dr. Kennicott's and De Rossi's MSS. למאס lemoes, "to him that despiseth his friend;" and hence the passage may be read: To him who despiseth his friend, it is a reproach; and he will forsake the fear of the Almighty: or, as Mr. Good translates, "Shame to the man who despiseth his friend! <div eID="gen16111" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16112" type="x-p"/> He indeed hath departed from the fear of the Almighty." <div eID="gen16112" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16113" type="x-p"/> Eliphaz had, in effect, despised Job; and on this ground had acted any thing but the part of a friend towards him; and he well deserved the severe stroke which he here receives. A heathen said, Amicus certus in re incerta cernitur; the full sense of which we have in our common adage: - <div eID="gen16113" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16114" type="x-p"/> A Friend in Need is a Friend Indeed. <div eID="gen16114" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16115" type="x-p"/> Job's friends, so called, supported each other in their attempts to blacken the character of this worthy man; and their hand became the heavier, because they supposed the hand of God was upon him. To each of them, individually, might be applied the words of another heathen: - - Absentem qui rodit amicum, <div eID="gen16115" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16116" type="x-p"/> Qui non defendit alio culpante; solutos <div eID="gen16116" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16117" type="x-p"/> Qui captat risus hominum, famamque dicacis, <div eID="gen16117" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16118" type="x-p"/> Fingere qui non visa potest; commissa tacere <div eID="gen16118" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16119" type="x-p"/> Qui nequit; hic niger est; hunc tu, Romane, caveto. <div eID="gen16119" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16120" type="x-p"/> Hor. Satyr. lib. i., s. iv., ver. 81. <div eID="gen16120" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16121" type="x-p"/> He who, malignant, tears an absent friend; <div eID="gen16121" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16122" type="x-p"/> Or, when attack'd by others, don't defend; <div eID="gen16122" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16123" type="x-p"/> Who trivial bursts of laughter strives to raise, <div eID="gen16123" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16124" type="x-p"/> And courts, of prating petulance, the praise; <div eID="gen16124" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16125" type="x-p"/> Of things he never saw who tells his tale, <div eID="gen16125" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16126" type="x-p"/> And friendship's secrets knows not to conceal; - <div eID="gen16126" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16127" type="x-p"/> This man is vile; here, Roman, fix your mark; <div eID="gen16127" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16128" type="x-p"/> His soul's as black as his complexion's dark. <div eID="gen16128" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16129" type="x-p"/> Francis.
entries.a7c4a40a93dde8f7dd1f87e03b6d8dfcdd6bf51c: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen16129" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16130" type="x-p"/> Have dealt deceitfully as a brook - There is probably an allusion here to those land torrents which make a sudden appearance, and as suddenly vanish; being produced by the rains that fall upon the mountains during the rainy season, and are soon absorbed by the thirsty sands over which they run. At first they seem to promise a permanent stream, and are noticed with delight by the people, who fill their tanks or reservoirs from their waters; but sometimes they are so large and rapid as to carry every thing before them: and then suddenly fail, so that there is no time to fill the tanks. The approach of Job's friends promised much of sympathy and compassion; his expectations were raised: but their conduct soon convinced him that they were physicians of no value; therefore he compares them to the deceitful torrents that soon pass away.
entries.76d070f60d38239e5f3cce16f4d1dada4be847ca: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen16130" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16131" type="x-p"/> Blackish by reason of the ice - He represents the waters as being sometimes suddenly frozen, their foam being turned into the semblance of snow or hoar-frost: when the heat comes, they are speedily liquefied; and the evaporation is so strong from the heat, and the absorption so powerful from the sand, that they soon disappear.
entries.c81d7023725f13fbfe6048838d23bf67d43539e3: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen16131" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16132" type="x-p"/> The paths of their way - They sometimes forsake their ancient channels, which is a frequent case with the river Ganges; and growing smaller and smaller from being divided into numerous streams, they go to nothing and perish - are at last utterly lost in the sands.
entries.76b4db3cadb07af32175c6460717dec1b325eb76: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen16132" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16133" type="x-p"/> The troops of Tema looked - The caravans coming from Tema are represented as arriving at those places where it was well known torrents did descend from the mountains, and they were full of expectation that here they could not only slake their thirst, but fill their girbas or water-skins; but when they arrive, they find the waters totally dissipated and lost. In vain did the caravans of Sheba wait for them; they did not reappear: and they were confounded, because they had hoped to find here refreshment and rest.
entries.841ebc0142cd7406460f1aab5320f15d8d6814b2: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen16133" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16134" type="x-p"/> For now ye are nothing - Ye are just to me as those deceitful torrents to the caravans of Tema and Sheba; they were nothing to them; ye are nothing to me. Ye see my casting down - Ye see that I have been hurried from my eminence into want and misery, as the flood from the top of the mountains, which is divided, evaporated, and lost in the desert. <div eID="gen16134" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16135" type="x-p"/> And are afraid - Ye are terrified at the calamity that has come upon me; and instead of drawing near to comfort me, ye start back at my appearance.
entries.6c6e10ccfc4d3502c44e7db5f890e01f8d4e35a5: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen16135" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16136" type="x-p"/> Did I say, Bring unto me? - Why do you stand aloof? Have I asked you to bring me any presents? or to supply my wants out of your stores?
entries.e79a274b2dd7d51b80baa0bc67709029b99e34dd: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen16136" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16137" type="x-p"/> Or, Deliver me - Did I send to you to come and avenge me of the destroyers of my property, or to rescue my substance out of the hands of my enemies?
